newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia to woo fresh funds on new management only.
newsitem.headline: Serbia to woo fresh funds on new management only.

text.p: Serbia's upcoming privatisation will woo foreign investment only if companies change their management along with selling shares to the people, Western economists said on Wednesday.

"The new draft privatisation law is good news for foreign investors, but foreigners will not buy the privatisation story from Serbia unless it is accompanied by changes in management," a London-based investment banker told Reuters.
"A privatised company must be really private with changed managerial structure. Otherwise it won't function," the banker added.
Along with privatisation which must create strong private companies, Serbia needed to create a real market and make its bourse functional, said the banker who asked not to be named.
"But the moment Yugoslavia lets private parties manage a bank, foreign capital will start flowing in," the banker said and added that nobody wanted to deal with the state banks.

While waiting for some foreign capital to come to its industries desperate to kick-start idling factories running at an average 30 percent of installed capacities, Yugoslavia said it had asked a foreign bank to help it boost confidence in local banking system and again attract savings to the banks.

"We have asked one foreign bank to initiate a project in Yugoslavia to help restore confidence in the local banking system. Right now we are doing a feasibility study and expect an answer soon," general manager of the Beogradska Banka system Borka Vucic told Reuters.
Sources close to the Beogradska banka banking group said the job was offered to Societe General Belgrade office. But a Societe General representative said: "We know nothing about that."

"If any respectable foreign bank puts its name in such a project to woo new savings, than the foreign bank will appoint its own chairman and make independent decisions on where to invest savings," another foreign banker said.

Wooing fresh savings was a burdensome task for the state which in 1991 froze over four billion dollars in individual hard currency savings. The final blow came after two large savings pyramids collapsed in 1993.
Economists unofficially estimate that Yugoslavs still hide almost three billion German marks in their mattresses and had no intention of depositing money with banks.
Funds will be more than welcome for an economy which is performing badly with almost 50 percent of the workforce out of jobs and without fresh capital to raise production and exports.
But to attract new savings meant the government had to tackle a thorny issue of paying back frozen savings.
New Yugoslav finance minister Bozidar Gazivoda said frozen savings had been spent a long time ago for the needs of the economy and it was the state's responsibility to repay.

"There are various mechanisms to pay back. We can go for fresh borrowing on international capital markets, direct some privatisation receipts to service the debt or employ some fiscal mechanisms," he said.
However, fresh external borrowing was out of question until Yugoslavia rejoined the International Monetary Fund (IMF), economists said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
